questions.stem: Why do hotels and villas repair linen instead of throwing it away at the first small fault?
options: Because guests like to see mended items
Because damaged linen cannot be washed again
Because new linen is not sold in Jamaica

questions.stem: When should a damaged item NOT be repaired?

essays.stem: Explain why a hotel or villa repairs and recycles its linen. Give at least three reasons.
essays.modelAnswer: Linen such as sheets, towels, napkins and uniforms costs a lot of money to buy. A small repair, such as re-stitching a hem or sewing on a button, makes an item last much longer, so the property spends less on new stock. Repairing faults early also stops a small tear from becoming a big one in the wash. Guests expect neat, clean linen with no holes or loose threads, so removing and fixing damaged items keeps the property's standard high. When linen is too worn to repair, recycling it into cleaning rags, laundry bags or dust sheets means the property does not need to buy as many cloths, and less waste goes to the dump. This helps the environment, which is important for Jamaica's tourism. Keeping records of repaired and condemned items also helps the property plan its stock.
markingPoints: Saves money: repaired items last longer and less new stock is bought
Early repair stops small faults getting worse
Keeps the standard guests expect
Recycling gives useful cloths and bags and cuts waste for the environment
Records help plan and control stock

essays.stem: Describe how you inspect laundered linen and sort it into items to use, to repair and to condemn.
essays.modelAnswer: I wash my hands and work at a clean table with good light. I check each item as I fold it. I look over both sides for stains, tears, holes, loose or broken hems, missing buttons and pulled threads. I hold sheets and pillowcases up to the light to find thin patches and small holes. Items in good condition are folded and put in the clean stock to use. Items with a small fault that can be fixed, such as a loose hem, a missing button or a small hole, go in the repair pile. Items that still have stains after re-washing go back for stain treatment once, as the property says. Items that are worn thin, badly torn or stained for good are condemned. I record the repair and condemned items on the linen sheet and tell my supervisor.
markingPoints: Clean hands, clean table and good light
Checks both sides for stains, tears, holes, hems, buttons and pulled threads
Holds items up to the light to find thin patches
Sorts correctly into use, repair, re-wash and condemn
Records the items and reports to the supervisor

essays.stem: Describe, step by step, how you re-stitch a loose hem on a sheet or towel by hand.
essays.modelAnswer: First I check that the item is clean and dry. I choose a thread that matches the colour and type of the fabric, and a needle that suits its thickness. I cut a length of thread about as long as my arm, thread the needle and tie a small knot at the end. I fold the hem back along the old fold line and hold it with pins, with the pin points away from my fingers. I start a little before the loose part, on the inside, so the knot is hidden. I sew small, even hemming or slip stitches along the hem, catching only a few threads of the main fabric so the stitches hardly show. I finish a little past the loose part with a few small stitches on top of each other, and trim the thread. I take out the pins, press the hem and check it.
markingPoints: Checks the item is clean; chooses matching thread and a suitable needle
Folds the hem on the old line and pins it safely
Starts before the loose part with the knot hidden on the inside
Sews small, even stitches that hardly show
Secures the end, removes the pins, presses and checks

essays.stem: Explain how to use an electric sewing machine safely.
essays.modelAnswer: Before I start I check the cable and plug for damage, and I do not use the machine if they are damaged. I place the machine on a firm table with good light, and I keep the cable where nobody can trip over it. I switch off and unplug the machine before I thread it, change the needle or the foot, or clean out lint. I keep my fingers flat on the fabric, well away from the needle, and let the feed dogs move the fabric instead of pulling it. I keep long hair tied back and loose sleeves and jewellery away from the moving parts. I keep my foot off the pedal when I am not sewing. When I have finished, I lower the needle into a scrap of fabric or the plate, switch off, unplug and cover the machine, and follow the maker's instructions.
markingPoints: Checks the cable and plug before use; firm table, good light, no trip hazard
Switches off and unplugs before threading, changing parts or cleaning
Keeps fingers away from the needle and does not pull the fabric
Ties back hair; keeps sleeves and jewellery away; foot off the pedal when not sewing
Switches off, unplugs and stores after use, following the maker's instructions

essays.stem: Describe how to put a patch over a hole in a staff uniform so the repair is neat and strong.
essays.modelAnswer: I check the uniform is clean. I choose patch fabric of the same type and colour as the uniform, and wash it first so it will not shrink later. I trim any loose threads around the hole. I cut the patch so it is about 2 cm bigger than the hole on every side, with straight edges, and I fold the edges under, or plan to zigzag them so they do not fray. I place the patch on the inside of the garment, or on top if the property prefers, line up the grain of the fabric and pin or tack it in place. I sew around the edge with small, even stitches by hand, or a straight or zigzag stitch on the machine, and secure the ends. I take out the tacking and pins, press the patch and check that it lies flat.
markingPoints: Uses matching fabric, washed first
Trims the hole and cuts the patch about 2 cm larger on every side
Stops the edges fraying (folded under or zigzagged)
Pins or tacks it in place with the grain lined up, then sews evenly and secures the ends
Removes pins and tacking, presses and checks it lies flat

essays.stem: Describe how you turn condemned towels into cleaning cloths, and how you keep them separate from guest linen.
essays.modelAnswer: I use only condemned towels that have been washed and that have been recorded on the condemned linen list and approved by my supervisor. I lay each towel flat on a clean table and mark it out into squares of the size the property uses, for example about 30 cm by 30 cm. I cut along the lines with sharp fabric shears, keeping my other hand away from the blades. I sew round the cut edges with a zigzag stitch or a hem, so they do not fray in the wash. I mark the cloths clearly, for example with a coloured stitch, a stamp or a dye, so that nobody puts them back into guest rooms. I count them, record the number made, and store them with the cleaning supplies, away from the clean guest linen, as the property says.
markingPoints: Uses only washed, recorded and approved condemned towels
Marks out and cuts safely to the property's size
Finishes the edges with zigzag or a hem so they do not fray
Marks or dyes the cloths so they are not used as guest linen
Counts, records and stores them away from guest linen

essays.stem: Explain why records are kept of repaired and condemned linen, and say what the records should show.
essays.modelAnswer: Records show the property how much linen is being damaged, repaired and lost, so the manager can order new stock in time and keep the par stock at the right level. They also help the property spot problems. For example, if many towels from one delivery have the same fault, the supplier can be told, and if many sheets are torn in one area, the cause can be found, such as a damaged bed frame or a faulty washing machine. Records stop linen from going missing without anyone knowing. A good record shows the date, the type of item, how many, the fault found, whether it was repaired, re-washed or condemned, what it was recycled into, and the name or signature of the staff member and the supervisor who approved it.
markingPoints: Helps keep par stock and order new linen in time
Shows patterns of damage so causes or suppliers can be dealt with
Controls losses and missing linen
Shows date, item, number, fault and action taken
Signed by the staff member and the supervisor

essays.stem: Explain the hygiene and safety points to follow when you sort, handle and repair linen.
essays.modelAnswer: I wash my hands before and after handling linen. I only repair linen that has been laundered. If I find linen with blood or body fluids on it, I wear gloves and deal with it as the property's procedure says, and I never shake it. I lift linen bags with bent knees and a straight back, keep the load close, and ask for help with heavy bags. I keep pins and needles in a pincushion or closed box, never in my mouth, and I pick up any I drop. I carry scissors closed and pass them handles first. I switch off and unplug the sewing machine before threading or cleaning it. I work in good light and take short breaks to rest my eyes and back. If I use a stain-removal chemical, I read the label and the SDS, wear gloves and never mix products.
markingPoints: Washes hands; only repairs laundered linen
Uses gloves and procedure for blood or body fluids and never shakes it
Lifts safely and gets help with heavy loads
Stores pins and needles safely and handles scissors safely
Machine safety, good light and safe use of chemicals (label, SDS, gloves, no mixing)

essays.stem: Describe how you check that a repair is of a good standard before the item goes back into use.
essays.modelAnswer: I look at the repair on both sides of the item in good light. The thread should match the colour of the fabric and the stitches should be small, even and in a straight line. The ends must be secure, with no loose threads or knots on the right side. A hem should be the same width as the rest of the hem and lie flat. A patch should be flat, with no puckers, and its edges should not fray. A button should be firmly sewn on and line up with its buttonhole. I gently pull the repaired area to check that it is strong. I trim any loose threads, then press the item. If the repair is not good enough, I undo it with a seam ripper and do it again. I record the repair and return the item to the clean stock.
markingPoints: Checks both sides in good light
Matching thread; small, even, straight stitches
Secure ends; no loose threads; hem, patch or button correct and flat
Tests the strength gently, then trims and presses
Redoes a poor repair; records it and returns the item to stock

essays.stem: Describe, step by step, how to sew a flat button back onto a uniform by hand so that it stays on.
essays.modelAnswer: I find a button that matches the others in size, colour and number of holes, and a strong thread that matches the uniform. I cut about 60 cm of thread, double it through the needle and tie a knot. I find the right place from the old holes or by closing the garment and marking through the buttonhole. I make a small stitch on the right side where the button goes, to hold the knot. I put the button on, and lay a pin or a matchstick across the top of it so the button will not be sewn too tight. I sew up and down through the holes about six times. I take out the pin, bring the needle out under the button and wind the thread round a few times to make a shank. I finish with a few small stitches on the back, and trim the thread.
markingPoints: Chooses a matching button and strong matching thread, doubled and knotted
Finds the correct position
Uses a pin or matchstick to leave space for a shank
Sews through the holes several times and winds a shank
Finishes securely on the back and trims the thread

practical1.title: Inspect, sort and record a batch of linen, and make hand repairs
practical1.brief: The Centre gives the group a batch of about 20 clean, laundered linen items (sheets, pillowcases, towels, napkins and uniforms). Some have faults: loose hems, a missing button, small holes, pulled loops, stains and items worn thin. As a group, set up a clean, well-lit work table. Each member inspects at least four items, says what they found and sorts each into "use", "repair", "re-wash" or "condemn", and the group records every item on a linen inspection sheet. Then each member makes at least two hand repairs on items from the repair pile: re-stitch a loose hem, and either sew on a button or darn a small hole. Each member checks another member's repair and presses the finished items. Photograph each stage below and add the photos and the completed inspection sheet to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: About 20 clean linen items with faults set up by the Centre
Hand-sewing needles, thread in matching colours, thimbles, pins and pincushions
Fabric scissors, seam rippers and tape measures
A linen inspection sheet and pens
An iron and ironing board, and labelled baskets for use, repair, re-wash and condemn
photos: The clean work table set up with tools and labelled baskets
A member holding a sheet up to the light to check for holes
The four piles sorted, with labels
A hem being re-stitched, with the pins in place
A sewn-on button or a darned hole, close up
checklist: Washed hands and set up a clean, well-lit work area
Inspected both sides of each item and found the faults correctly
Sorted each item correctly into use, repair, re-wash or condemn
Recorded each item correctly on the inspection sheet
Chose matching thread and a suitable needle for each repair
Made a neat, secure hem repair with small, even stitches
Sewed on a button firmly with a shank, or darned a hole neatly
Kept pins and needles in a pincushion, handled scissors safely and cleaned up
safety: Keep pins and needles in a pincushion; never hold them in your mouth; pick up any you drop
Carry scissors closed and pass them handles first
Switch off the iron when not in use and keep the cable clear of the floor
Wash hands before and after handling linen

practical2.title: Make machine repairs and turn condemned towels into cleaning cloths
practical2.brief: Set up and check an electric sewing machine (or two, if the Centre has them) with the assessor watching. Each member makes one machine repair on an item the Centre provides: re-sew a split seam on a pillowcase, or put a patch over a hole in a uniform or a tablecloth. Then the group recycles condemned towels: record them on the condemned linen sheet with the "supervisor's" signature, mark them out into cloths about 30 cm by 30 cm, cut them, zigzag or hem the edges, and mark the cloths so they cannot be mistaken for guest linen. Each member cuts and finishes at least three cloths. Count and record the cloths made and store them as the Centre says. Finish by cleaning and putting away the machine safely. Photograph each stage below and add the photos and the completed records to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: An electric sewing machine with spare needles, bobbins and thread
Items to repair: pillowcases with split seams and uniforms or tablecloths with holes
Patch fabric (washed) to match the items
Fabric shears, tape measures, tailor's chalk, pins and pincushions
A condemned linen sheet, a recycling record and pens
Fabric marker or coloured thread for marking the cloths
photos: The machine checked: cable and plug sound, machine threaded
A seam being re-sewn or a patch being stitched
The finished machine repair on both sides
Condemned towels recorded and signed on the sheet
Towels marked out and cut into squares
Cloths with zigzagged or hemmed edges, and their marking
The finished cloths counted and the recycling record filled in
The machine switched off, unplugged, cleaned and covered
checklist: Checked the cable and plug and threaded the machine correctly with it switched off
Kept fingers away from the needle and let the machine feed the fabric
Secured the seam ends by sewing back over them
Made a neat, flat machine repair (seam or patch) with matching thread
Recorded the condemned towels and got them signed before cutting
Cut the cloths safely to size and finished the edges so they will not fray
Marked the cloths so they cannot be used as guest linen
Counted and recorded the cloths, and cleaned and stored the machine safely
safety: Switch off and unplug the machine before threading, changing the needle or cleaning
Keep fingers, hair, sleeves and jewellery away from the needle
Keep the machine cable off the floor and away from where people walk
Cut with sharp shears on a table, keeping the other hand clear of the blades
Keep pins and needles in a pincushion and pick up any that fall
